newsitem.title: USA: GM working to recover from impact of strikes.
newsitem.headline: GM working to recover from impact of strikes.

text.p: General Motors Corp reported lower 1996 fourth quarter operating earnings due to strike-related production losses, said Tuesday the giant automaker continues to rebuild its strength.

"Clearly our 1996 fourth-quarter and calendar-year results were impacted by the strike-related production losses in the United States and Canada and are not indicative of GM's potential for continued profit improvement," said GM Chairman and Chief Executive Officer John Smith Jr. "We continue to rebuild our strength in North America and grow our business in key international markets throughout the world." he said.
GM's 1996 fourth quarter income from continuing operations totaled $786 million or $0.92 a share compared with $1.6 billion or $1.95 a share in the fourth quarter of 1995.

Fourth quarter results were reduced by an estimated $700 million after taxes or $0.91 a share, due to strike-related work stoppages in the United States and Canada, which resulted in the temporary shutdown of some GM North American assembly and component plants during the quarter. Work stoppages in the United States and Canada reduced calendar-year earnings on an after-tax basis by about $1.2 billion, after considering partal recovery of production losses from the work stoppages.

Smith said GM has the flexibility to continue its drive to become the industry's low-cost competitor. "We recognize that we face significant challenges, but we're well-positioned to follow our strategy of utilizing common parts and processes, while implementing lean operations, to compete on a global basis, and grow the business in all of our sectors," he said.

He said production start-ups in 1996 for new models ran according to plan and were much better than those in 1994 and 1995. "We have more new cars and trucks going into the market now than any time in the last 15 years," Smith said.

About 20 percent of the 1997 production will be for the new models launched in 1996. "Those new cars and trucks are key to our plans to aggressively increase market share in the United States this year," he said in a statement.

Smith said GM has begun the largest international production-capacity expansion in the company's history with major new manufacturing and assembly facilities planned for key international regions. "Those facilities will provide us with significant opportunities to leverage GM's global resources and enhance our competitive position throughout the world," he said.
During 1996, GM started production at its assembly facility in Russia and continued work on new manufacturing and assembly plants in Argentina, China, Poland and Thailand.
